column1: processor-reserve-withheld-sales-income|A reserve holdback is not automatically a reduction of sales. Reconcile the underlying transactions and evaluate your rights to the held money under the processor agreement and tax accounting method. Bank payouts alone do not establish taxable receipts.|An online retailer has strong December sales, but the processor withholds a percentage for possible chargebacks. The owner records only cash deposited and loses track of the reserve. Build the sales-to-payout bridge before deciding whether the holdback changes income timing.|Reconcile gross transactions, adjustments and reserve movements;Read withdrawal restrictions and ownership terms;Track later releases without recording the same sale again|Processor agreement;Monthly settlement reports;Reserve ledger;Sales and refund records|A later reserve release can duplicate revenue if the original sale was already recognized.|A reserve the processor owns under a genuine dispute differs from funds merely withheld as collateral. Give the advisor the actual restrictions, not only the account's reserve label.|Keep a reserve rollforward showing beginning balance, additions, uses and releases. Ask the preparer to document any timing adjustment separately from the financial reconciliation.

chargeback-cross-year-1099k-sales|Match the chargeback to the original sale, then determine the proper year and type of adjustment from the actual facts and accounting method. A processor's current-year reporting does not automatically require rewriting the original sale-year return.|A customer disputes a November purchase in February. The retailer previously reported the sale, and February's settlement reduces the bank payout. The current reconciliation must retain both the old transaction reference and the new chargeback date.|Locate the original sale and its prior reporting;Separate the refunded sale amount from dispute fees;Reconcile current settlements and any corrected information return|Original order;Chargeback notice;Both years' processor reports;Filed sales workpaper|Subtracting the chargeback from sales and deducting it again as a separate expense counts the same reversal twice.|A temporary dispute hold differs from a final reversal. Preserve the resolution date and any amount recovered after appeal instead of treating every notice as an irreversible customer refund.|Request a two-year transaction bridge that shows the original receipt, current reversal, fees and final result. Use the applicable return method to assign the tax adjustment.

processor-backup-withholding-owner-tax-credit|Federal backup withholding is generally a tax payment to reconcile, not an ordinary processing expense. Identify the payee and return entitled to the credit, and keep the withholding separate from gross sales and merchant fees.|A provider reduces the store's deposits after a taxpayer-information issue. The bookkeeper posts the reduction to card fees. The information form and payee identity should establish how the withheld tax reaches the correct return.|Identify reported federal withholding and payee details;Reconcile tax withheld separately from transaction fees;Coordinate any correction and credit with the preparer|Form 1099-K;Payer notices;Merchant statements;Entity and owner return information|Deducting withholding as a merchant fee can understate profit and fail to claim the actual tax payment correctly.|A fee charged by the processor differs from tax remitted to the government. Match the amounts to the information form rather than assume every payout deduction is a business cost.|Request a gross-sales, fees-and-withholding bridge and evidence supporting the credit. Have the payer correct inaccurate taxpayer details through its process instead of silently moving the credit between returns.

processor-bankruptcy-unpaid-merchant-funds|Determine the legal claim, prior income recognition, tax basis and recovery prospects before claiming a loss. A failed processor does not automatically make the entire screen balance deductible in the failure year.|A retailer has customer receipts and reserve funds trapped when a processor enters bankruptcy. The merchant may recover part through the estate or insurance. The advisor needs to distinguish sales already recognized from contingent amounts and unsupported dashboard balances.|Reconcile the claim to transaction records and prior reporting;Document rights in held funds and expected recoveries;Evaluate applicable loss or bad-debt rules and timing|Processor statements;Bankruptcy notices;Filed claim;Prior income and reserve workpapers|Deducting lost profit or an amount never included in tax basis can overstate the actual deductible loss.|Segregated funds held for a merchant may create different rights from an unsecured claim against the processor. Obtain the contract and claims information before treating every unpaid dollar identically.|Prepare a claim-basis and recovery schedule. Track distributions from the estate and any later reimbursement against the same workpaper so a supported loss is not counted twice.

platform-pays-vendor-from-gross-sales|A net payout is not automatically net revenue. Determine whether your business is selling goods as principal or arranging a transaction as agent, then account for supplier payments consistently with that relationship.|A platform collects customer payments and pays a fulfillment supplier before remitting the remainder to the store. The owner calls the remainder commission income even though the store sets prices and bears customer obligations. Review the actual contracts before adopting that label.|Identify the seller and party responsible to the customer;Reconcile gross customer charges and supplier invoices;Separate supplier costs, platform fees and agency amounts|Platform terms;Supplier agreement;Customer invoices;Settlement detail|Deducting supplier invoices after reporting only a net margin can understate profit through a second deduction.|A genuine sales agent may have different rights from a merchant outsourcing fulfillment. Product custody and payout mechanics alone do not determine which arrangement exists.|Ask for a documented principal-versus-agent conclusion and a gross-to-net ledger template. Use the same treatment across sales channels with equivalent contracts.

marketplace-coupon-platform-funded-discount|Identify who funds the coupon and what the seller is entitled to receive. A discount borne by the marketplace can differ from a seller-funded price reduction; reconcile the order economics before reducing sales.|A customer pays less after applying a promotional code, but the marketplace reimburses the seller for the coupon. The settlement also contains fees. The seller should distinguish customer cash, platform funding and the amount actually sacrificed by the store.|Read promotion and reimbursement terms;Match coupon funding to each order;Separate seller discounts from marketplace subsidies or other payments|Promotion agreement;Order detail;Platform funding report;Settlement statements|Subtracting a coupon from revenue when the seller was reimbursed can understate the transaction.|If the seller bears part of the promotion, split the contributions using the agreement. A campaign banner saying platform promotion is not enough to identify who ultimately paid.|Retain a promotion-level reconciliation and ask the preparer to classify any platform incentive separately where appropriate. Compare it with reported gross payment totals.

customer-tips-passed-through-processor|Track tips separately from business sales while preserving complete payroll and payment records. Removing them from owner revenue does not eliminate employer reporting or the obligation to distribute the money correctly.|A service business receives one daily card settlement containing service charges and voluntary staff tips. The owner records the full deposit as sales, then deducts tip distributions without reconciling payroll. Gross receipts, employee amounts and fees need a common bridge.|Identify voluntary tips versus mandatory service charges;Reconcile amounts received and distributed by employee;Coordinate wage and tip reporting with payroll|Point-of-sale reports;Tip allocation records;Payroll registers;Processor settlements|Mandatory service charges should not automatically follow the treatment used for voluntary customer tips.|If the business retains an amount or determines its distribution, tell payroll exactly how the arrangement works. The screen's tip label does not settle every wage and employment-tax question.|Maintain a tip liability reconciliation tied to payroll and bank activity. Have the provider confirm reporting from the actual compensation arrangement.

foreign-processor-currency-conversion-sales|Keep the sale amount, conversion and processor charge identifiable. The net domestic-currency deposit alone may conceal fees and exchange differences that belong in separate parts of the reconciliation.|A seller invoices overseas customers in euros. The provider converts each payout after deducting fees, while the owner's sales software uses a different rate. The books need a consistent translation approach and a trace from each order to its settlement.|Preserve original-currency sales and settlement dates;Separate conversion charges from exchange differences;Apply a consistent supported tax translation method|Foreign-currency invoices;Processor rate detail;Bank deposits;Refund and conversion reports|Treating every difference between invoice and deposit as a processing fee can hide actual currency movements.|A sale invoiced in dollars but paid through a foreign bank differs from a foreign-currency receivable. Establish the currency of the obligation before deciding how exchange changes arise.|Ask the preparer for a documented currency policy and a sample reconciliation. Keep original data so a later refund can be matched to the correct transaction.

processor-account-closed-final-reserve-release|Trace the release to the taxpayer and reserve balance from the original sales. Closing the storefront or changing the deposit account does not establish that the release is new personal income or a new sale.|A retailer winds down in December, then receives reserve funds the following spring. The owner deposits the payment personally and forgets the entity's closing ledger. The release must be reconciled with prior sales, chargebacks and the company's wind-down records.|Identify the original merchant and reserve owner;Determine how the underlying receipts were previously reported;Coordinate the release with final or continuing entity reporting|Closed processor account statements;Reserve rollforward;Prior returns;Distribution and dissolution records|Recording the release as both current sales and repayment of a reserve duplicates one receipt.|A reserve previously recognized as part of sales differs from an amount whose tax inclusion was properly deferred. Preserve the original method conclusion rather than inferring treatment from the release date alone.|Ask the preparer to update the closing workpaper and owner accounts. Confirm remaining fees or chargebacks before considering the processor relationship fully settled.

processor-fee-rebate-after-yearend|A rebate of processing fees generally needs to be connected to the original expense treatment. It is not automatically a reduction of current sales. Review whether the prior deduction produced a tax benefit and identify the appropriate recovery treatment.|A processor credits a retailer after correcting last year's fee rate. Current payouts include both new customer sales and the old fee rebate. The bank deposit should be broken into those components rather than booked entirely as current revenue.|Identify the fee periods corrected;Reconcile prior deductions and actual tax treatment;Separate fee recovery from current sales and new fee charges|Rate agreement;Rebate calculation;Prior fee ledger;Current settlements|Reducing current sales by an old fee refund can move an expense correction to the wrong reporting line.|A prospective discount on new processing differs from repayment of fees charged in a prior year. Ask the provider which transaction occurred instead of inferring it from one net credit.|Maintain a fee-recovery bridge and give the preparer the original deduction history. Reconcile any corrected payer statement without inventing an expense to force annual totals to match.

supplier-rebate-inventory-already-sold|Relate the rebate to the purchases that earned it and your inventory method. A supplier payment may adjust product cost rather than represent unrelated income, with a split needed when some goods remain unsold.|A wholesaler receives an annual volume rebate covering inventory bought throughout the year. Most products sold, but some remain on hand. Posting the whole check to miscellaneous income loses the connection between the rebate, cost of goods sold and remaining stock.|Identify qualifying purchases and the rebate terms;Allocate supported adjustments between sold and retained goods;Apply the business's tax inventory method consistently|Rebate agreement;Purchase history;Year-end inventory;Supplier credit statement|Reducing current purchase cost and separately booking the same rebate as income can double count the benefit.|A genuine payment for marketing services differs from a purchase-price rebate. Identify what the supplier is paying for rather than treating all vendor credits as the same transaction.|Prepare a purchase-cost reconciliation showing the rebate's effect and retain the allocation method. Have the preparer review any cross-year adjustment using the filed accounting method.

supplier-minimum-purchase-shortfall-fee|Read the contract to determine what the fee buys or settles. A shortfall charge may differ from a deposit applied to future purchases, a price adjustment or a payment securing a longer-term right.|A retailer commits to buy a minimum quantity annually. It buys less and pays a charge that the supplier may credit against next year's orders. The possible future credit matters when evaluating both the expense and the commercial obligation.|Identify whether the payment is final or creditable;Separate current purchases from future contractual rights;Review timing under the applicable accounting method|Supply agreement;Shortfall calculation;Payment receipt;Future-credit terms|Calling every shortfall charge a penalty does not establish current deductibility or eliminate a continuing asset.|A permanently forfeited contractual payment differs from an amount recoverable through future orders. Document the conditions for recovery instead of expensing the payment based only on its invoice label.|Ask for a contract-based classification and track any available credit. Reconcile later purchases so the same payment is not deducted again when applied.

custom-inventory-customer-cancels-order|A canceled order does not automatically make its goods worthless or permit an arbitrary write-off. Review ownership, remaining sale or salvage value and the inventory method before changing cost of goods sold.|A manufacturer builds branded products for a customer who cancels. Some units can be reworked, others have scrap value, and the customer owes a cancellation charge. The loss analysis should distinguish those outcomes instead of eliminating the entire batch at cost.|Document condition and realistic disposition options;Separate cancellation recovery from inventory value;Apply the supported inventory valuation or disposal treatment|Production costs;Cancellation agreement;Rework and scrap estimates;Disposal or later sale evidence|The expected profit on the canceled order is not the same as the tax basis lost in the goods.|An intention to discard products differs from completed disposal or an allowed valuation adjustment. Preserve evidence of what happened to each material category rather than relying on a year-end management estimate alone.|Request a batch-level cost and recovery workpaper. Keep later sales, scrap proceeds and customer payments linked so the final result does not duplicate a previously recognized loss.

inventory-stored-overseas-yearend-title|Determine ownership and risk under the purchase and shipping terms, not just physical location or payment date. Goods at a port can belong to different parties depending on the contract.|A business prepays an overseas manufacturer in December. Goods reach the port but do not clear customs until January. The inventory count, payable or deposit entry and insurance should follow a supported ownership analysis rather than whichever date gives the preferred deduction.|Read delivery and title provisions;Reconcile shipping, acceptance and customs dates;Match owned goods to the inventory and cost records|Purchase contract;Bill of lading;Shipping terms;Insurance and customs documents|Prepayment does not by itself prove that the buyer owned finished goods before year-end.|An advance on unfinished production differs from payment for completed goods whose ownership already transferred. Ask the supplier for status evidence rather than treating every shipment as one identical in-transit purchase.|Prepare an in-transit inventory schedule approved by the preparer. Record the basis for inclusion or exclusion and reconcile it when the shipment arrives.

supplier-tooling-charge-mold-stays-factory|Review the rights purchased, expected benefit and contract terms. Paying for tooling that remains at a supplier does not automatically make it your owned equipment or an immediate inventory expense.|A product business pays a manufacturer to create a custom mold. The supplier keeps physical possession and can use it only for the buyer's orders. Ownership, usage rights and future unit pricing matter more than where the mold sits.|Read title, exclusivity and termination provisions;Separate tooling rights from product purchase costs;Review capitalization and recovery from the actual agreement|Tooling contract;Supplier invoice;Ownership and usage provisions;Expected production and termination terms|Expensing the tooling fee and then including it again in each unit's inventory cost can duplicate the same spending.|A mold owned by the buyer differs from a supplier-owned tool covered by a production commitment. Document what happens if the relationship ends, including removal, destruction and compensation rights.|Request a cost-and-rights memo tied to the supply contract. Give the preparer the usable-life and ownership evidence before placing the payment on either an equipment or inventory schedule.

inventory-warranty-replacement-cost|Track the replacement's actual cost and how the original product was accounted for. A free replacement is not a new cash sale, but the inventory movement and any supplier reimbursement still need support.|A retailer replaces defective units without charging customers. The warehouse removes replacement stock and accounting also posts a warranty expense from the same report. Without reconciliation, the same cost can reach deductions twice.|Trace original and replacement inventory movements;Separate actual costs from reserves or estimated future claims;Track supplier credits and customer recoveries|Warranty terms;Replacement log;Inventory cost records;Supplier reimbursements|A reserve for expected future replacements and costs already incurred require different timing analysis.|A cash refund, repair service and stock replacement create different records. Identify which remedy occurred so the tax workpaper does not use a generic warranty entry for every claim.|Create a claims-to-inventory reconciliation and review the accounting method with the preparer. Compare the expense ledger with cost of goods sold before filing.

bulk-spare-parts-equipment-inventory|Classify parts by their actual use and characteristics rather than putting every purchase into inventory or expensing the entire shipment. Resale stock, repair supplies and major replacement components can require different treatment.|A service business purchases routine consumables, an expensive backup assembly and parts intended for customer resale on one invoice. The company needs separate categories tied to use instead of a single year-end tax deduction.|Separate resale items from internal-use parts;Identify costs requiring capitalization or special supplies treatment;Track installation, consumption and unused balances|Itemized invoices;Parts usage history;Fleet records;Stock count and installation dates|An expensive part sitting on a shelf is not automatically treated like a low-cost consumable used immediately.|A component installed to improve equipment can differ from one used in routine maintenance. Preserve what the work accomplished, not only the part number, so the advisor can evaluate the actual repair or asset transaction.|Request an item-category policy and reconcile the initial purchase to later use. Keep resale cost records distinct from equipment and maintenance schedules.

customer-supplied-manufacturing-materials|A customer's materials do not automatically become your inventory or revenue merely because they enter your premises. Establish ownership and the service being sold, then record any materials your business actually purchases separately.|A fabricator processes metal supplied by its customer and charges a conversion fee. The warehouse count includes the customer's metal, while the bookkeeper proposes assigning it purchase cost. Custody records should distinguish customer property from company-owned inputs.|Confirm ownership and loss responsibility in the contract;Separate processing fees from goods the company sells;Maintain customer-property counts outside owned inventory|Manufacturing agreement;Customer material receipts;Production usage records;Company purchase invoices|Counting customer property as an owned asset can inflate inventory and create unsupported costs.|If the agreement actually transfers materials in payment or as part of an exchange, the analysis changes. Have the advisor review that arrangement rather than assuming every customer delivery remains someone else's property.|Keep a custody reconciliation and document the revenue model. Confirm how scrap, excess materials and damaged customer property are settled before the first year-end count.

inventory-packaging-returnable-containers|A reusable container may need separate asset or supplies treatment instead of being charged to every product sale. Track ownership, customer deposits, expected use and actual losses before choosing the cost treatment.|A distributor ships products in durable containers that customers return. Accounting expenses the container with each shipment even though it is reused many times. Customer deposits also appear in revenue without a separate liability analysis.|Identify whether title transfers to customers;Track reusable units, deposits and losses;Review capitalization and cost recovery separately from product cost|Container purchase records;Return terms;Deposit ledger;Container movement log|A returned container should not create a fresh acquisition cost merely because it ships with another order.|Disposable packaging sold with goods differs from an asset the business expects to recover. Refundable customer security also differs from a purchase price; separate both questions in the workpaper.|Ask for a container and deposit rollforward with a supported expense or asset policy. Reconcile write-offs to actual loss evidence and later recoveries.

demo-inventory-converted-business-use|When products leave resale stock for sustained business use, review whether their cost moves to a business asset or another supported category. An internal transfer does not create a sale to the owner.|A retailer installs stock permanently in a demonstration room. The products are used for customer presentations for several years instead of being available for ordinary sale. The inventory ledger and any depreciation schedule need to agree on the conversion.|Identify which units permanently changed use;Establish supported cost and readiness for business use;Review asset recovery and any later sale separately|Inventory cost records;Demonstration plan;Installation date;Subsequent use or sale history|Leaving the cost in inventory while also depreciating it duplicates the same basis.|A temporary display of goods still held for sale differs from durable equipment removed from stock. Document how sales staff and management actually treat the items rather than relying only on a display-room location.|Request a dated reclassification and basis schedule. If a demonstration unit is later sold, connect the disposition to that schedule instead of treating the full receipt as an unrelated inventory sale.

barter-services-equipment-business-income|Receiving equipment for services can create business income even without a cash payment. Establish the value and receipt timing, then record the equipment's basis and recovery separately. A noncash deal does not remove either side of the transaction.|A consultant accepts a customer's used production machine in satisfaction of an invoice. The consultant plans to use the machine in the business and wants to book no income because nothing reached the bank. The service receipt and asset acquisition need separate support.|Document the service obligation settled;Support the equipment's fair market value;Record asset basis, business use and any applicable recovery|Invoice;Written exchange agreement;Valuation evidence;Equipment transfer and use records|Deducting the machine while omitting the service income can misstate the economics of the exchange.|If the equipment only secures an unpaid bill rather than transfers in payment, the facts differ. Establish legal ownership and the amount actually settled instead of treating every delivered asset as completed compensation.|Prepare a noncash receipt and acquisition workpaper. Reconcile the customer's account and the fixed-asset schedule so later depreciation or sale uses supported basis.

customer-dispute-retainage-never-received|A cash-method review asks when payment was actually or constructively received, while an accrual-method review can produce a different timeline. An invoice alone does not settle the timing of disputed retainage.|A contractor completes work in December, but the customer withholds a contractual amount pending defect review. The contractor has not received the money and cannot draw it. Distinguish a genuine unresolved right from money made available but voluntarily left untouched.|Confirm the filed tax method and contract terms;Document the dispute and restrictions on payment;Track resolution and eventual receipt separately|Contract;Retainage calculation;Dispute correspondence;Payment and acceptance records|Writing off retainage as bad debt after never including it in income can create an unsupported deduction.|Funds available on demand differ from an amount the customer can still refuse under an unresolved claim. Supply the advisor with actual access and acceptance facts rather than only the invoice date.|Ask for a contract-level timing conclusion and maintain the balance until resolved. Reconcile later settlements to the amount originally recognized, if any.

subscription-customer-credit-future-services|An internal credit does not necessarily create a current deduction simply because it reduces a customer's future bill. Review whether it is a refund obligation, price concession or future service right and apply the business's tax method.|A subscription company offers a service credit after an outage. No cash is returned, and customers can apply the credit only on renewal. The company should separate financial-statement reserves from amounts actually paid or reflected in tax income.|Read redemption and expiration terms;Identify whether the customer has a present refund right;Track credits issued, used and expired by period|Service agreement;Credit notices;Redemption ledger;Revenue method workpaper|Deducting the full credit when issued and reducing revenue again when redeemed counts the concession twice.|An unconditional cash refund differs from a discount contingent on buying future services. The customer's rights can change timing even when both are described as goodwill credits.|Request a credit rollforward and a supported tax adjustment policy. Tie redemption to invoices so the same customer concession enters the return once.

gift-card-breakage-business-closure|Closing the business does not by itself extinguish customer rights or determine income timing. Reconcile the tax treatment of original card sales with refunds, redemptions and applicable unclaimed-property obligations.|A retailer stops trading with unused gift-card balances. Some customers request refunds and others cannot be located. The owner wants to reverse every liability without checking how the original receipts were reported or whether the obligation survives closure.|Reconcile outstanding balances to prior income reporting;Have counsel address continuing customer and unclaimed-property duties;Separate actual refunds from amounts still owed|Gift-card terms;Sales and redemption history;Prior tax workpapers;Closure and customer notices|Eliminating a book liability does not establish that the company can keep the cash or that a tax adjustment is required.|Cards already included in taxable receipts differ from properly deferred amounts. Preserve the original method and legal obligations rather than assuming closure produces the same entry for every balance.|Ask the preparer and counsel for a wind-down schedule connecting tax, refunds and remaining liabilities. Retain card-level evidence after the storefront closes.

customer-money-held-project-escrow|Escrow funding is not automatically income to every party named in the project. Determine ownership, restrictions and release conditions, then apply the recipient's accounting method to its actual rights.|A client puts a project's budget into an independent escrow account. The contractor receives payments only after milestones are approved and cannot withdraw the balance. The amount funded and the amount the contractor is entitled to receive may differ.|Identify the escrow beneficiary and control rights;Document milestone approval and release dates;Separate client funds from receipts available to the business|Escrow agreement;Project contract;Milestone approvals;Escrow and bank statements|Reporting only releases without examining unrestricted access can be just as problematic as treating all escrow funding as immediate receipts.|An account labeled escrow but controlled freely by the contractor differs from an independent arrangement with real restrictions. Give the advisor the actual signature and withdrawal provisions.|Request a rights-and-release timeline supporting the income method. Reconcile each release to the relevant invoice and any retained client property.

nonrefundable-booking-fee-rescheduled-project|A nonrefundable advance can have different timing from a refundable security deposit. Rescheduling work does not automatically defer the receipt. Review payment rights, the business's tax method and any applicable advance-payment rules.|A service firm collects a booking fee in December and agrees to perform the project next March. The client cannot demand a refund but can reschedule. The owner should distinguish the unconditional payment from amounts still contingent on completing work.|Read refund, forfeiture and rescheduling provisions;Confirm the tax method for advance payments;Reconcile later invoices so the fee is not counted twice|Booking contract;Payment receipt;Rescheduling agreement;Advance-payment method records|Deferring every fee to the work date because the books show deferred revenue can misapply the tax method.|A customer right to a cash refund can change the analysis. Identify substantive rights rather than relying on a fee's marketing description or the label used by the scheduling software.|Ask the preparer to document the current-year treatment and later application. Keep tax and management-reporting adjustments visible when they differ.

customer-paid-bank-loan-on-behalf-business|A customer payment made to satisfy your business obligation can still be income from the sale or service. The absence of a deposit in your own account does not erase the transaction.|A client owes a contractor for completed work. At the contractor's direction, the client sends the payment to the equipment lender. The contractor should record both the customer settlement and the debt payment, including the principal and interest components.|Match the redirected amount to the customer invoice;Confirm the lender credited the business obligation;Separate revenue recognition from debt principal and interest|Payment instructions;Customer invoice;Lender statement;Loan amortization schedule|Treating the lender payment only as a reduction of debt can omit revenue; deducting all of it as interest creates another error.|A payment made as your agent differs from a customer independently paying its own obligation. Preserve the agreement showing whose debt was settled and why the customer received credit.|Prepare a noncash funds-flow entry supported by both parties' confirmations. Reconcile the loan balance and customer account without inventing a bank transaction that never occurred.

contract-buyout-for-lost-future-revenue|A cancellation payment is not automatically capital gain because the contract covered several years. Analyze the right surrendered and what the payment replaces, including ordinary future service revenue.|A software-services company receives a lump sum when a client exits a long-term support agreement. The company keeps its other customers and operating assets. The payment should be evaluated from the contract and settlement rather than called a business sale.|Identify the rights released and obligations terminated;Separate unpaid service fees, damages and other components;Coordinate the settlement description with return reporting|Original contract;Termination agreement;Payment schedule;Prior billing and income records|Applying a capital-gains rate to the whole payment before identifying the underlying right can understate tax.|A payment for selling a separate asset may differ from one replacing operating income. If the settlement includes both, seek a supported allocation instead of using a single convenient description.|Ask for a component-level character and timing analysis before signing. Preserve the commercial rationale alongside the final agreement and receipts.

settlement-customer-refund-plus-legal-fees|Separate the settlement components and determine the underlying obligation for each. A customer refund, fee reimbursement, penalty or acquisition of a right can have different treatment despite being paid with one check.|A business resolves a customer dispute by returning part of the purchase price and contributing to the customer's legal costs. The bookkeeper posts the total to refunds. The settlement agreement should establish what each component settles before classification.|Read the release and allocation;Match any refund to prior sales reporting;Evaluate other payments independently under the applicable rules|Signed settlement;Original invoices;Legal bills and allocation;Payment evidence|Calling the entire payment a sales refund can distort both gross receipts and the character of other amounts.|An agreement's labels are useful evidence but do not replace its substance. Have counsel explain the actual claims and rights released so the tax advisor can evaluate the payment from consistent facts.|Request an invoice-to-settlement bridge and supporting tax memo. Reconcile amounts already reserved or deducted so payment does not create a duplicate expense.

trade-credit-received-advertising-services|Usable barter or trade credits can create income before you spend them. Review when the credits become available, their value and restrictions rather than waiting automatically for a bank deposit.|A design firm accepts credits in a trade network for completed work. The credits can buy advertising from other members. The firm needs to report its service compensation and separately evaluate the advertising obtained later.|Document when credits become usable;Support their fair value and any restrictions;Track spending and information returns separately from earning|Trade agreement;Credit account statements;Service invoices;Redemption records|Recording an advertising expense without the related service income can omit the compensation side of the barter.|Credits usable immediately differ from a contingent promise with meaningful unresolved conditions. Tell the advisor about transfer rights, expiration and practical availability instead of treating every point balance as equivalent cash.|Maintain an earned-and-used credit ledger and reconcile it to the return. Confirm the treatment of later expiration or unused balances from the actual terms.

scorp-debt-forgiven-after-owner-sells-shares|The company's recognition date and S-corporation allocation rules matter, along with any valid elections and sale terms. Former ownership alone does not establish who reports the later cancellation income.|A founder sells shares in July, and the company settles bank debt in September. The purchase agreement assigns some economic responsibility to the seller, but the K-1 allocation must follow the applicable tax rules and documented elections.|Establish when cancellation income is recognized;Review shareholder dates and any closing-of-books election;Separate contractual reimbursement rights from tax allocations|Stock sale agreement;Debt settlement;Ownership dates;Entity return and election records|A buyer-seller agreement allocating economic cost does not automatically rewrite who receives taxable income on a K-1.|A disposition of all shares can raise different election questions from a partial transfer. The entity preparer needs exact dates and consents before allocating income by an informal before-and-after spreadsheet.|Ask the entity and owner preparers for a consistent allocation memo. Reconcile the sale's indemnity or price provisions separately so contractual payments are not confused with tax ownership.

lender-chargeoff-debt-still-collected|A lender's accounting charge-off does not by itself prove that your legal debt was discharged. Review the actual cancellation event, collection activity and information reporting before removing the obligation from the tax books.|A bank marks a loan charged off, sells it to a collector and continues demanding payment. The business assumes the debt disappeared because of the statement notation. The transfer to another creditor needs to be distinguished from forgiveness.|Obtain the creditor's explanation of the account status;Read any release or settlement;Reconcile continuing collection and any Form 1099-C|Loan documents;Charge-off notice;Collection correspondence;Debt sale or release records|Writing off a payable solely because the lender stopped carrying it as performing debt can misstate outstanding obligations.|A binding discharge differs from a creditor changing its internal classification. If an information form conflicts with legal collection facts, bring both to the advisor rather than choosing whichever produces the preferred tax result.|Request a documented cancellation-date conclusion and retain correction correspondence where needed. Keep the liability reconciliation aligned with actual settlements and payments.

refinance-old-business-debt-fees-unamortized|Review the old financing costs separately from the new loan's costs. Refinancing may change the recovery of remaining costs, but a new note does not establish one universal immediate deduction.|A business replaces a bank loan before its original maturity. Its books still carry unamortized issuance costs, and the new lender charges additional fees. The advisor needs to know whether the old debt was extinguished, modified or continued.|Identify the legal debt transaction and lenders;Reconcile old unamortized costs and any write-off;Establish a separate schedule for new financing costs|Old and new notes;Payoff statement;Existing amortization schedule;Itemized fee invoices|Combining old remaining costs with new fees can obscure which financing each amount belongs to.|A modification with the same lender can raise different questions from an actual payoff and new borrowing. Provide the full agreements, not only the closing statement showing a new balance.|Ask for a debt-cost rollforward and transaction-specific recovery analysis. Keep principal, interest, prepayment charges and issuance costs identifiable in the books.

loan-origination-fee-withheld-proceeds|The amount withheld may represent financing costs, prepaid interest, a deposit or another charge. Receiving less cash than the note principal does not make the difference an immediate operating expense.|A lender approves a loan and sends the business the net proceeds after several fees. Accounting records only the cash deposit as debt. The debt balance and financing-cost schedule must instead reconcile to the actual obligation and charges.|Reconcile note principal to cash funded;Itemize each withheld amount;Review expense, capitalization and amortization treatment separately|Loan agreement;Funding statement;Fee invoices;Debt and cash entries|Recording the net deposit as the full liability understates the amount the business must repay.|A refundable holdback differs from a lender fee permanently charged.
